summary: MarsCraft is a free browser game in which children aged 7 to 12 run a crewed outpost on the floor of Gale Crater, Mars, and have to bring the crew home. It is a first-person block-building survival game a format children already know in which every useful action is paid for with another resource. One battery pays for breathable air, heating, the radiation shield, the greenhouse lights, the fuel plant, and the radio. One water tank is shared by drinking, farming, making oxygen, and the wall of the storm shelter. The numbers behind those choices are NASA measurements: the ground is a HiRISE
details:
does and how it works

MarsCraft is a first-person voxel game that runs in the browser, with no install or account. The player lands at an outpost in Gale Crater and follows a five-act story: call Earth, drive the rover to drill ice, survive a solar storm, grow food, and fuel the rocket before the launch window closes.

Every system shares the same limited supplies, so every choice has a cost:

- Energy: solar panels charge a battery only by day, at Mars' 43% of Earth's sunlight. Oxygen, the heater, the greenhouse lights, the radiation shield, the fuel plant and the radio all compete for it.
- Water: the same tank serves drinking, crops, and the shelter's water wall that blocks radiation.
- Radiation: when a solar storm is coming, the player either hides in the shelter and stops working, or powers the shield and drains the battery.
- Communication: asking Mission Control for advice costs energy, and the answer arrives after the real Earth–Mars signal delay for that date.

Real NASA data

- DONKI: solar storms come from real coronal mass ejections.
- RadLab (Curiosity): radiation doses are in real millisieverts.
- InSight: outside temperature and the weather report follow real readings by sol.
- HiRISE: the terrain is the real elevation of a crater inside Gale, at about one block per meter.
- OSDR: the greenhouse notebook shows real plant studies.

Sources are credited in-game. Embedded data shows its collection date, and only data fetched successfully is labeled "live".

Benefits and intended impact

Kids aged 7 to 12 learn engineering trade-offs by living them, not by reading about them. Short sentences, icons, animated "first time" moments and a final report card explain why each decision mattered. The goal is to make real mission constraints something a child can feel, and to spark interest in space science.

Tools

TypeScript, Three.js, Next.js, plain HTML/CSS, Three.js (3D engine) for the interface, Vitest for tests, and Vercel for hosting. A server route keeps the NASA API key out of the browser. Textures, models and icons are generated in code. Development was assisted by AI coding tools, as declared in the credits.

Creativity

It joins a block-building game kids already know with a real place and real data. The player walks the actual shape of Gale Crater, sees Earth, Phobos and Deimos in the Martian sky, and manages an NPC crew that also needs air, water and food.

What we considered

- Scientific honesty: a "Real vs Game" tab explains where game time is compressed.
- Cognitive load: one objective and one warning at a time.
- Access: phones are a first-class platform with full touch controls, and the game is in English, Portuguese and Spanish.
- Performance: it is tuned to run on modest devices.
